sections.title: Perimeter & Segmentation Defenses
sections.content:
Firewalls filter traffic by rules.
Stateless (ACL) filters per-packet; stateful tracks connections; NGFW adds app/user awareness + IPS.
A screened subnet (DMZ) isolates public-facing servers between two firewall boundaries.
Segmentation limits lateral movement: VLANs, subnets, and microsegmentation. Put untrusted/guest devices and IoT on their own segments.
ACLs permit/deny by source/dest IP, port, protocol — order matters (first match wins, implicit deny at the end).
Proxies, content filters, and a WAF (web application firewall) protect application traffic. IDS detects; IPS blocks in-line.
exam_tips: Stateful firewalls track connection state; NGFW adds application awareness + IPS.
A screened subnet/DMZ isolates internet-facing servers from the internal LAN.
ACLs are first-match with an implicit deny at the end — order the rules carefully.

sections.title: Access Control & Port Hardening
sections.content:
NAC (Network Access Control) checks a device's identity and posture (patches, AV) before admitting it, often with 802.1X.
802.1X — port-based authentication: the supplicant (client) authenticates to the authenticator (switch/AP) against a RADIUS authentication server before the port opens.
Switch-port hardening: port security (limit MACs), DHCP snooping (block rogue DHCP), dynamic ARP inspection (stop ARP spoofing), BPDU guard, disabling unused ports, and putting them in an unused VLAN.
Control plane: change default credentials, use role-based access control, and management out-of-band.
exam_tips: NAC verifies device identity + health posture before granting network access.
Harden access ports: port security, DHCP snooping, dynamic ARP inspection, disable unused ports.

sections.title: Hardening, Physical & Operational Security
sections.content:
Device hardening: change default passwords, disable unused services/ports, patch firmware, use secure protocols (SSH/HTTPS/SNMPv3), and enforce strong auth (MFA).
Physical security: locked racks/rooms, badge access, mantraps, cameras, cable locks, and asset tags — physical access can defeat most logical controls.
Encryption in transit (TLS, IPsec) and at rest; certificates and PKI establish trust.
Key management & logging: centralize logs (SIEM), keep time synced (NTP), and monitor for anomalies.
Honeypots lure and study attackers. Security policies + user training address the human layer.
exam_tips: Hardening basics: change defaults, patch, disable unused services, use SSH/HTTPS/SNMPv3, enable MFA.
Physical access can bypass logical controls — lock racks/rooms and control entry.
Encrypt in transit with TLS/IPsec; use PKI/certificates for trust.

concept_cards.hook: A firewall that tracks active connection state and automatically permits return traffic for sessions it allowed.
An isolated network segment for public-facing servers, separated from the internal LAN by firewall boundaries.
Port-based network access control where a supplicant authenticates through the switch/AP to a RADIUS server before the port is opened.
Network Access Control — admits devices only after verifying identity and security posture (patches, AV, config).
Access Control List — ordered permit/deny rules filtering traffic by IP, port, and protocol, with first-match and an implicit deny.
A switch feature that validates ARP packets against DHCP snooping data to block ARP spoofing.
Fine-grained network segmentation that isolates workloads from each other to limit lateral movement after a breach.
Reducing attack surface by changing defaults, patching, disabling unused services/ports, and using secure protocols + MFA.

practice_questions.q: What are the three roles in 802.1X authentication?
practice_questions.explanation: The supplicant (client) authenticates via the authenticator (switch/AP) to a RADIUS authentication server.

practice_questions.q: Which switch feature blocks rogue DHCP servers?
practice_questions.explanation: DHCP snooping only trusts DHCP replies from approved ports, blocking rogue servers.

practice_questions.q: Where should public-facing web servers be placed relative to the internal LAN?
options: Directly on the internet with no firewall
practice_questions.explanation: A screened subnet/DMZ isolates internet-facing servers from the internal network behind firewall boundaries.

practice_questions.q: Which control admits devices only after checking identity and security posture?
practice_questions.explanation: NAC verifies a device's identity and health (patches, AV) before granting network access.

practice_questions.q: Which switch feature validates ARP replies against DHCP snooping data?
practice_questions.explanation: Dynamic ARP Inspection drops forged ARP packets, defeating ARP spoofing.

practice_questions.q: Where should an organization place its public web and mail servers?
practice_questions.explanation: Public-facing servers belong in a screened subnet/DMZ isolated from the internal LAN.

practice_questions.q: Which solution checks a laptop's patch level and antivirus before allowing it on the network?
practice_questions.explanation: Network Access Control enforces posture checks (patches, AV) before granting access.

practice_questions.q: A firewall rule list ends with no explicit allow for unmatched traffic. What happens to it?
options: It is denied by the implicit deny
It is sent to the DMZ
practice_questions.explanation: ACLs end with an implicit deny, so traffic not explicitly permitted is dropped.
